note: The ship catalogue, returned by list_ships. Two tiers. A flown ship carries the published numbers for a real spacecraft, with a source for each one, and an unknown is left null rather than filled in. A speculative ship is a cargo hauler that does not exist: its engine performance is taken from a real thruster, its structure is invented, and it says so. Nothing in this file is a guess dressed as a measurement.

tiers.flown: A real spacecraft that has launched. Published specifications.
tiers.in_development: A real spacecraft a real company is building. Specifications mostly unpublished.
tiers.speculative: Not a real ship. Real engine performance, invented structure. This is where the mining scenario lives.

scale_warning: Every asteroid spacecraft ever flown has returned a sample measured in grams. OSIRIS-REx brought back 121.6 g and it holds the record. Commercial mining tonnage is not a bigger version of these missions, it is a different thing, which is why the haulers are marked speculative.

ships.name: OSIRIS-REx
ships.status: Launched 2016, dropped its sample capsule in Utah in September 2023, flew on as OSIRIS-APEX.
ships.notes: The record holder. It touched Bennu for about five seconds, blew nitrogen at the surface and caught what floated up. The head holds two kilograms by design and it came home with 121.6 grams, double what the mission required.

sources.dry_mass_tons: NASA OSIRIS-REx fact sheet, 880 kg unfueled
sources.propellant_capacity_tons: Spaceflight101 mission design analysis, 1095 kg of hydrazine
sources.cargo_capacity_tons: TAGSAM sample head design capacity, about 2 kg
sources.isp_s: Aerojet Rocketdyne MR-107S, rated 225 to 236 s, midpoint used
sources.capital_cost_usd: NASA Office of Inspector General life cycle cost, 1.1214 billion USD
sources.extraction_rate_kg_s: Model figure. The real collection was one five second touch, not a rate.
sources.transfer_time_multiplier: Model figure, not a published specification.

ships.uncertainty: Sources disagree on the masses. NASA's fact sheet says 880 kg dry and 2110 kg wet, Spaceflight101 says 860 kg dry and 1955 kg wet, the Planetary Society lists 1529 kg at launch. Cost runs from 1.0 to 1.16 billion USD depending on whether launch, operations and the extended mission are counted.

ships.name: Hayabusa2
ships.status: Launched 2014, returned its Ryugu capsule to Australia in December 2020, still flying toward another target.
ships.notes: Four ion thrusters producing 28 millinewtons between them, about the weight of a paperclip, running for years on end. It fired a copper slug into Ryugu to expose fresh material and caught 5.4 grams across two touchdowns.

sources.dry_mass_tons: Derived: about 600 kg at launch, less 66 kg of xenon and 48 kg of chemical propellant
sources.propellant_capacity_tons: 66 kg of xenon per the spacecraft table; a JAXA paper gives a 60 kg plan
sources.cargo_capacity_tons: Set to what it actually brought home, 5.4 g. The requirement was more than 100 mg.
sources.sample_returned_kg: NASA, 5.4 g of Ryugu across two samples
sources.isp_s: JAXA engineering paper, 2740 to 2890 s in flight. The thruster is rated 3000 s.
sources.capital_cost_usd: No published lifecycle figure found. Left null rather than estimated.
sources.extraction_rate_kg_s: Model figure. The real collection was a touchdown, not a rate.
sources.transfer_time_multiplier: Model figure for low thrust transfer, not a published specification.

ships.uncertainty: Launch mass is quoted as 600, 609 or 610 kg depending on the source, so the derived dry mass carries that spread. Specific impulse fell as the thrusters aged.

ships.name: Psyche
ships.status: Launched October 2023, on its way to the metal rich asteroid 16 Psyche. An orbiter: it carries no sampler.
ships.notes: The largest electric propulsion spacecraft sent beyond the Moon and the closest thing flying to a metal prospector. It brings nothing home, because it cannot: there is no hold on it at all.

sources.dry_mass_tons: Wikipedia, 1648 kg. No official NASA dry mass figure found.
sources.propellant_capacity_tons: JPL press kit, seven tanks holding 1085 kg of xenon
sources.cargo_capacity_tons: Zero. It is an orbiter with no sample mechanism.
sources.isp_s: SPT-140 Hall thruster, 1800 s and 280 mN each, four fitted
sources.capital_cost_usd: Planetary Society estimate, 960.6 million USD total
sources.transfer_time_multiplier: Model figure for low thrust transfer, not a published specification.

ships.uncertainty: JPL gives up to 2747 kg at launch including the optical communications demonstrator, Wikipedia says 2608 kg. Xenon is quoted both as 1085 kg capacity and 922 kg loaded.

ships.name: Vestri
ships.status: Being built. Aiming to land on a metallic asteroid, probably 2022 OB5, launching with Intuitive Machines IM-3 in late 2026 or 2027. Its predecessor Odin was lost after launch in 2025.
ships.notes: The only real commercial asteroid mining spacecraft here, and the one we know least about. Its plan is to land and refine on the surface rather than haul rock home. Ask the engine to plan a mission with it and it will refuse, because the numbers are not public.

sources.dry_mass_tons: Space.com, about 200 kg, roughly twice the mass of Odin
sources.exhaust_velocity_m_s: Not published. Described only as an electric motor with landing gear.

ships.uncertainty: Almost everything. A company building hardware does not publish a specification sheet, and the launch date has already slipped once.

ships.name: Methalox Shuttle
ships.status: Does not exist. A cargo hauler on a chemical stage, for the mining scenario.
ships.notes: Fast and simple, and it pays the rocket equation in full on the way home with the ore aboard. Expect it to run dry on anything but the easiest targets, which is exactly why it is in the list.
ships.basis: The specific impulse of 360 s is typical of a flown methalox upper stage. The hull, the hold, the cost and the life are invented.

sources.isp_s: Real, flown methalox upper stage class

ships.name: Hall Tug
ships.status: Does not exist. A cargo hauler on Psyche's thrusters, for the mining scenario.
ships.notes: The middle of the list and usually the right answer. The thruster is the SPT-140 that Psyche actually flies, scaled into a bank; the freighter around it is invented.
ships.basis: The specific impulse of 1800 s is the real SPT-140 figure, the thruster flying on NASA Psyche. The hull, the hold, the cost and the life are invented.

sources.isp_s: Real, SPT-140 as flown on NASA Psyche

ships.name: Ion Freighter
ships.status: Does not exist. A bulk hauler on Hayabusa2 class thrusters, for the mining scenario.
ships.notes: Sips propellant and hauls the heaviest loads, and takes half again as long to get anywhere. It is the only ship here that pays for a trip to a high delta v target. The thruster performance is Hayabusa2's, measured in flight; the freighter around it is invented.
ships.basis: The specific impulse of 2800 s is the in flight figure measured on Hayabusa2's mu10 thrusters. The hull, the hold, the cost and the life are invented.

sources.isp_s: Real, JAXA mu10, 2740 to 2890 s in flight
